utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. And good afternoon to everyone. For the record all the accused are here. From the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Haynes, Mr. Bourgon and Mr. Ostojic. Prosecution has strengthened its team, it seems. They have got Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Nicholls, Mr. Thayer, but I also see two new faces. Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, we are joined today by Nicole Janisiewicz, and Moya Magilligan who are helping today. Unfortunately Ms. Stewart couldn't be here today. She had to return home suddenly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's fully understandable. I thank you, Mr. Nicholls, for keeping the Trial Chamber informed. I understand that there are some preliminaries here, preliminary issues you wish to raise. Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. Good afternoon. There is a preliminary matter I would ask the Chamber to enter an order to see sequester Mr. McCloskey from this hearing due to the fact that the witness who is coming to testify, who was the -- who was an investigator who allegedly or purportedly took statements in question, and I know you all have not looked at those statements, but I can tell you that about 75 per cent of the questioning was done by Mr. McCloskey in the first interview, and approximately 60 per cent or thereabouts in the second. And I may very well, and I think I will call him as a witness and that being the case, and I've talked to Mr. McCloskey about this this morning, and so I just ask that he be sequestered. If he's going to be a witness, then he shouldn't be allowed really to listen to what Mr. Graham testifies concerning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Meek. Does anyone wish to respond to that, either Mr. Nicholls or Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll go first. I strongly object to that. There hasn't been any ground given other than this I may call him as a witness. I don't know first of all, why he -- why Mr. Meek would have any reason to call Mr. McCloskey as a witness when we have the investigator who was present during the entire recording. And second, since we have a transcript of the interview and we have audio of the interview, it's no secret what went on in that interview, and I'd like to know why and for what purpose he intends to call him as a witness because if it's a whim of his, I'm not going to agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, very simply, Your Honour, I do intend to call him as a witness and while it may very well be easy for Mr. Nicholls to say that the investigator was present the whole time during the questioning or the entire recording, there are instances, Your Honour, where Mr. McCloskey was not in the presence of the investigator. However, he was in the presence of the -- and with Mr. Borovcanin's lawyer outside -- that's not taped -- and that's approximately 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I see no reason why that would make Mr. McCloskey a witness. Lawyers always talk during interviews, lawyers talk before court, after court. The fact that Mr. McCloskey was sometimes talking with Mr. Borovcanin's lawyer, still that's a very cryptic reason and ground for sequestering the senior trial attorney and saying you're going to call him as a witness. If he needs a witness to those conversations, I don't know why he doesn't approach the other party who was not a party to this case, who was not -- I don't know whether he has talked to the lawyer who was present at the time but that would clearly obviate the need, if there is any need at all anyway, for Mr. McCloskey to be a witness or to leave this room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Take your time, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour, the reason that Julian Nicholls is taking this witness and not Peter McCloskey is very evident and that reason is is that Peter McCloskey is too close to these interviews and that's why he's sitting in the back chair and not questioning this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, I was just about to say usually we would prefer to hear it from the horse's mouth. I'm not attributing equine -- anything equine or equine to you Mr. McCloskey, but I see that you are volunteering a statement. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Meek's last statement is simply not true. The reason that Mr. Nicholls is handling this is just for simplicity because we've heard earlier that there were may be allegations that were made and it's much simpler this way. We are not acknowledging or suggesting or agreeing that there is anything untoward about being involved in an interview. This Tribunal and this -- the OTP was founded upon the principle that a lawyer was in the investigating team from the very beginning of this Tribunal. I was that lawyer in the Srebrenica case and have been always that lawyer. It was absolutely necessary and appropriate for me to be involved in taking these interviews. So there is nothing wrong with that. Today we have a burden to show you that this was a free and voluntary interview. We would like to get on with it and the allegations and the other issues, I don't know where this is coming from, and there has been no legal grounds suggesting I need to be part of anything that has been put forward. This appears to be an effort just to drag one of the lawyers through the system, which would be a real problem because in any system it's crucial for prosecutors to be able to speak to counsel for witnesses, counsel for accused, and be able to do it freely, to discuss what, as you know as a former Defence counsel, is discussed in all systems, and if either side, either Defence lawyer or Prosecutor is going to be dragged without any grounds except that I intend to call him as a witness, this puts a terrible chilling effect on the ability for lawyers to talk with other lawyers about the legal matters that are so important. So I am of course here ready to serve the Court and -- but we would like some kind of solid grounds before we go any further in this area and we would like to get on, we brought Mr. Graham here and we're ready to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Just one final word, Your Honour, and that is this hearing is a hearing regarding the admissibility of a statement of a co-accused or an accused in this case but it's a two-pronged step, and if you find that it was -- it is admissible, the second question that you need to reach is, is it admissible only against Mr. Borovcanin or is it admissible against any other accused he may have mentioned? And that therein lies the problem that I believe Your Honours should sequester Mr. McCloskey because I am going to call him as a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Remaining on the team of horses, actually, in my mind, I am thinking that we may be putting the cart before the horse to an extent. Let me explain why. Let's go to the ultimate move that Mr. Meek is hinting at, namely, that at some later point in time, not only does he intend now, but he is sure that he will summon you as a witness, Mr. McCloskey. Do you think that your presence today or your absence from the courtroom today would make a difference when we come to that stage? One reason that I can mention to you is, for example, that one of the usual practices, although it's not an absolute one, is that if a witness has been present during the testimony of -- during the hearing of evidence in a trial, usually that could amount to an obstacle from then bringing him forward or her forward as a witness, which would in turn affect the idea or the intention that Mr. Meek is intimating as a present to have, namely of summoning you, and that's why he is asking for you to be sequestered, I would imagine. I'm just putting it to you whether you have given this due consideration, whether it would be a major obstacle for you to absent yourself from the courtroom voluntarily, not as a result of a sequestration from the Trial Chamber for the duration of Mr. Graham's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do I get a room at the Dorint and witness fees? Your Honour, I wouldn't give that three thoughts. I wouldn't leave this courtroom until ordered. I don't -- if Mr. Meek could provide me with some sort of background on why I could be a witness; for example, if it were some sort of fact situation where I happen to run across something in the -- in this crime, but being present during a taped interview of an accused is something that lawyers and prosecutors have done every month of every year that this Tribunal has been in existence, and if we have to leave because of the -- this kind of dramatics that is being pulled here, no. If he can tell me where he's going and what the purpose of this is and if it's something that you think is -- has foundation, I will voluntarily leave, of course, but I can't imagine what it is. To me, this is just something that happens occasionally in my system. It's usually to get the Prosecutor off the trial so a new one comes on. I've reviewed my -- the ethics of my bar association and had this been a jury trial and I could be a witness, then I would be obligated to leave. It says with a court trial I'm not, interestingly enough. I think they think judges can handle this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think in most jurisdictions you would be able to give testimony without the need to renounce to the brief, if I can use the word renounce to the brief, because I don't think it's appropriate in your case but yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, Judge, Mr. McCloskey intimates that I'm doing this in some fashion to get him off of the case and have a new Prosecutor come in and that's just simply not true. I'm just asking, and you know how many witnesses we've had so far, and different prosecutors have interviewed them but this is a special case. And I'm note asking he be recused for the entire case, I'm just asking for this one witness. Now if what Mr. McCloskey wants me to do is to tell him what questions I'm going to ask him, I don't think that's appropriate. I don't think I should be made to do that. And he knows -- he's a good lawyer, he's a bright lawyer, he's been around, he know what I'm going to ask him about in substance and I've already mentioned it in open court already. But it's up to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. The other thing that I would like to mention that is -- is that I think there is a big difference between counsel being summoned as a witness, who already, who in any case, even if he's absent from the courtroom, has access to the transcript in any case, and an ordinary witness who is summoned and in no way, unless there is an abuse of the process, would he have at his disposal transcript of the testimony. That is also a difference that I think you ought to keep in mind, if you wish to -- one moment because I am stuck here. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, of course I envisioned that the possibility that if Mr. McCloskey wouldn't do the right thing and agree to leave, which he's now said he won't, and if you sequester him, I would hope that as honourable as he is, he wouldn't go right back and start listening to this testimony or reading the transcripts. He frankly can sit in the witness room where there is no access to it and I assume, I presume, that would be part of the order; that he not listen to the proceedings nor that he listen to the LiveNote or read the LiveNote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He is responsible for the Prosecution in this case. He's responsible for the Prosecution. And technically speaking, if the interrogation or the questioning is going to be conducted by Mr. Nicholls, as lead counsel for the Prosecution, supposed to be, let's put it in quotes, supervising Mr. Nicholls, and directing him on what questions to put or what not to put. I mean, it's -- he's in a different position than an ordinary witness. Anyway, this is something of course that we will need to discuss. We'll have a short break when we come to that before we start with the testimony of Mr. Graham.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: I just had a question, Mr. Meek, just looking at -- you indicate that you've already advised us as to the relevance of Mr. McCloskey's purported or proposed testimony, but I'm not clear on what that was. Are you suggesting that what you'd want to have him testify to is not what went on in the interview room with Mr. Borovcanin but what went on with Mr. Borovcanin's lawyer outside the interview room? You're saying that's relevant to what went on inside the interview room? And do I have you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, you do have me correct. You do have it correctly. One is the issue of what happened outside the "interview," and the second issue is what went on during the interview, because again and you can ask Mr. McCloskey, he'll verify what I say, that the primary interrogator was not Mr. Graham, it was Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: But you're not disputing, Mr. Meek, that what went on in the interview room is in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No, I'm not disputing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any further preliminaries on your part? Can you wait, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, it's on a completely different subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why I asked you because I guessed so. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Should you know, I have no knowledge that Mr. Bubic, the lawyer, is being called as a witness or has been interviewed by anyone. I've spoken to Mr. Lazarevic about that, and they have no intention of calling Mr. Bubic or challenging any of this. So I don't think you go through the Prosecutor on an issue like this. That's not your first line of defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish to respond to that, Mr. Meek and we close the discussion here please on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour. First off, if we had a ruling right now that the interview itself, if admissible, is admissible only against the party making the statements, then I wouldn't be standing here. I'd have no objection whatsoever. However, whether or not the counsel who was present on that day will be called as a witness, we haven't come to our Defence case yet, number 1, and number 2, that's what's looming over this whole proceeding is whether there is any probative value to any statements made by Mr. Borovcanin, if it's admissible at all will be admissible against any other co-accused. If you made the ruling that it's not going to be, and those parts would be redacted, I'll sit down and shut up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I want to dispel from your mind any idea you might have that this issue of admissibility is going to be dealt with in two stages, now and later on, when we arrive at the defence stage. I mean, that's not what we have in mind for sure. We are going to deal with the admissibility issues related to the Borovcanin statement, alleged statement, we exhaust all the evidence that we have. Yes, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Obvious a very brief issue, I would just like to confirm that I had the discussion with Mr. McCloskey, and indeed we have no intention to bring Mr. Bubic to give evidence and of course not Mr. McCloskey either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I think we will come back to you on this after a short break that we will have when we finish with other preliminaries. Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I wrote a few days ago to Mr. Cubbon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm coming to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm grateful. Then I think I'll sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't want to abruptly stop you there, but I think it will save us a few minutes. I'll come straight to that, in fact. We were informed by Mr. Cubbon with regard to the Prosecution motion for leave to amend the 65 ter list, Exhibit list, with intercept corroborating documents, which was filed on the 6th of July, that notwithstanding the fact that on the 9th of July I invited all Defence teams to respond to the -- that motion by the end of last week, if possible, then transpired that you had missed the fact that I had suggested this deadline, and you are asking for permission to be able to file your response by the close of business of tomorrow; if -- I stand corrected if that is not so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour. Your Honour has encapsulated it perfectly. We were in error. I will say in fairness that Your Honours had couched it not in terms of an order but as a preferable course. I'm afraid we have not adopted the preferable course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And you may have noticed also that I had -- I was using more or less words which reflect precisely what I was supposed to have stated on the 9th of July in any case. So, yes, permission is granted, permission is granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We are also informed that, having received all these responses you wish to file a reply to -- or a response to the Defence responses? Is that the correct information that we have received?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Mr. Vanderpuye has a brief response on some of the issues that were brought up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. In that case we can fix a deadline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Then assuming you would have received Mr. Josse's reply by the 18th, you have up to the 20th to file that. One thing we want to make clear is that this matter will not be decided before the recess but only after. All right. Ms. Nikolic, you will recall that over the past week, you know exactly what I'm talking about, I'm referring to your urgent motion for urgent disclosure of all Rule 68 material. You had intimated that roughly you were expecting the final material from the Prosecution at least on two or three occasions last week. If you could please enlighten us on -- update us on this issue?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Good afternoon. All the material that we requested from the Prosecution has been submitted by now so we withdraw our urgent motion for disclosure, and I believe all the further requests would be dealt with between the parties without your intervention. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. So we'll take note of that. You don't need to file anything. One moment. Yes. The Borovcanin Defence team, on the 3rd -- I'm not sure about the date. Yes, on the 3rd of July, 2007, filed confidentially a request for certification of an interlocutory appeal against our decision on Prosecution's confidential motion for testimony of Witness 88 to be heard via videolink. Under normal circumstances, our decision, which is going to be oral in this case, would have been given in private session, but in our decision we will not be making any reference to who this person is or to where he now lives or where he lived, so we can dispose of the motion for certification in open session. So as stated we are seized of this Borovcanin Defence team motion. We note that the granting of certification is discretionary and in the hands of the Trial Chamber, and that Rule 73(B) sets forth that certification may be granted by a Trial Chamber if the decision impeached involves an issue that would significantly affect the fair and expeditious conduct of the proceedings or the outcome of the trial and for which in the opinion of the Trial Chamber, an immediate resolution by the Appeals Chamber may materially advance the proceedings. The Trial Chamber considers that the manner by which Witness 88 will give testimony does not significantly affect the fair and expeditious conduct of the proceedings or the outcome of the trial, for that matter, since the Defence's right to cross-examination will not be affected and neither will the broader right to a fair trial. Further, the test for videolink applications is whether it would be in the interest of justice, taking into account the particular circumstances of -- in each instance. The decision therefore being particular to its facts does not affect the overall conduct of the trial proceedings. For the same reasons, the Trial Chamber does not consider that an immediate resolution by the Appeals Chamber of this issue would materially advance the proceedings. Consequently pursuant to Rules 54 and 73(B) of the rules we hereby dismiss the request for certification. One moment. I need to consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are other matters that we need to communicate to you but I think we need to take a short break now to discuss the matter raised by Mr. Meek, and we hope to be back with you within a short time. Thank you. --- Break taken at 2.51 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's dispose first of the matter raised by Mr. Meek. This is of course an oral decision and it will not be followed by a written one. The first premise of our decision is predicated on the very nature of the practice in this Tribunal, which is particular, namely, that officers of the Office of the Prosecutor prosecuting in a trial would normally have been involved personally in the investigation stage, and in the interview of prospective witnesses and suspects. This is, as I said, particular to this Tribunal and any comparison with common law and civil law practices, which vary greatly, would in our opinion be futile. This fact calls for particular attention when a Trial Chamber is dealing with motions like the one you made, Mr. Meek, on behalf of the Beara Defence team today, because of the broader impact it would have, the outcome of such motion could have. Given the practice in this Tribunal and the submissions made, we do not see any valid reason to sequester Mr. McCloskey during the testimony of Mr. Alistair Graham. Further and finally we wish to point out that any intention on the part of a counsel to summon Mr. McCloskey as a witness would have to be the subject of an ad hoc motion. So that clears up that issue from our table. Now you will recall that we have had lengthy discussions on the issues related to the testimony of Mr. Alistair Graham and the alleged Borovcanin statement. We have already informed you that later on, first we will proceed with the testimony of Mr. Graham, limited to admissibility matters or issues, and later on we will need to decide, and we will decide, on the admissibility of the alleged Borovcanin statement vis-a-vis Mr. Borovcanin himself. We would also have to decide on the admissibility of the same alleged statement vis-a-vis any or all of the other accused. However, the arrival of Mr. Alistair Graham here has been preceded also by two motions by the Prosecution, seeking leave to add some documents to the 65 ter list, I'll be referring to them very shortly and very succinctly, and a number of responses to the same motions. Basically what is being questioned is the admissibility of these documents on the grounds that, first, they should not be included in the 65 ter list for reasons that have been propounded in the various responses; and secondly, and for that reason, that the Prosecution should not be allowed to make use of them during the testimony of Mr. Alistair Graham. We are talking of two transcripts disclosed to the Defence on the 22nd of September, to audio recordings, and more or less the discussion on these four documents is -- has been more or less superseded by the decision that we have already taken allowing the Prosecution to make use of them in the course of the testimony of Mr. -- and the Defence, not just the Prosecution, testimony of Mr. Graham. Then five employment records relating to Mr. Borovcanin which were disclosed to the Defence on 3rd of July, four documents created by Mr. Borovcanin during one of the interviews which were disclosed to the Defence on the 3rd of July of this year, one DVD shown to Mr. Borovcanin during one of the interviews which was disclosed to the Defence on the 26th of June of this year, four documents chronicling the efforts to interview Mr. Borovcanin which was disclosed to the Defence on the 3rd of July. Then, on this -- all this was the subject of the Prosecution motion of the 6th of July of this year. Then six days after, that's on the 12th of July, the Prosecution filed a second motion seeking leave to supplement its previous motion by seeking to have added to the 65 ter list a further three documents from Republika Srpska that further chronicle the Prosecution's efforts to interview Mr. Borovcanin. We have seen the two motions. We have also seen all the responses received from Mr. Borovcanin himself, from Miletic and Beara Defence teams, and others. I don't need to repeat them all. We have given these motions and responses a lot of thought and on behalf of the Trial Chamber I wish to thank you for all the work and the time you dedicated in preparing them and filing them. We have given them a lot of thought, and the final decision that we have arrived at is that at this stage, with the information that we have, it is somewhat premature for us to decide definitively on whether to include them in the 65 ter list or not. But on the other hand, there is an impelling need to proceed with the testimony of Mr. Graham, and we believe that while we reserve our position to decide on the Prosecution, two Prosecution motions in due course, for the time being, while leaving that issue unprejudiced, we will allow, permit, the Prosecution to make use of any of these documents that it might wish to make use of, subject, of course, to any ultimate decision that we may take after we have had more -- given more thought and considerations to the various submissions that have been made. And later on, of course, we will come down with our decision, which will be in writing. Okay? So I don't think there is anything else preliminary to Mr. Graham being admitted to the courtroom. Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, if I understand you well, then, the Prosecution is allowed to use the exhibits that are still pending the motion, including the entire transcripts and the entire audio? In this hearing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's put it like this: Those four documents, two transcripts and two audios have already, in a way, been dealt with by our previous decisions. You will recall that Mr. McCloskey initially asked to be able to play certain excerpts. We have disposed of that in the way we have. Implicitly, we were already telling the Prosecution, if you need to make use of this document, the audio, with the witness, you're free to do so but very limitedly within the parameters we have stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The rest, in other words, leaving alone the two transcripts, two audio recordings, we are saying, at the moment we think it's premature on our -- it would be premature on our part to pre-empt the issue and decide before Mr. Graham takes testimony. The understanding is that granting the Prosecution use of these other documents for the purpose of what the witness is going to testify doesn't mean that they have admitted these documents from the back door or from a window instead of from the front door. That ultimately will be decided and whatever happens today will be without prejudice to what we can ultimately decide on whether these documents ought to form part of the 65 ter list, and therefore whether they could be made use of. Obviously if we decide against including them in the 65 ter list, there will be consequences but the understanding is that what is happening today is with that knowledge, aforeknowledge, that could misfire, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So I just want to make sure, the portions that they are allowed to use go to the issue of the admissibility or voluntariness only? Correct? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's how I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I be clear about this? What the Chamber is about to embark upon is a voir dire. Will this evidence be evidence in the trial proper?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well it's a trial within a trial. It's part because it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's make this clear because as you know I think this is one Chamber where we have equal representation from the systems, and therefore, while a voir dire -- the voir dire concept is easily digested by me, for instance, that's not the case with others. So our common position is as follows: That although we fully understand what you mean, Mr. Josse, that basically we are looking at this rather than from the strict perspective of a voir dire as one further stage in the development of this trial. Later on we will take a decision which will first cover the issue of admissibility and if there is a decision in favour of admissibility, then the next stage would be what weight to give to the testimony. So you may or may not call it a voir dire, but we consider it as an integral part of these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And if I could excuse this shorthand, this is only to do with voluntariness and the such like at this stage?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are talking of -- I think we went through this last time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The issue that is Mr. Lazarevic outlined, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We went through this last time. There may be other issues of admissibility that we sort of agreed will not be the subject matter of Mr. Graham's testimony. In other words, we were limiting it to what Mr. -- because I think Mr. McCloskey himself rose last time and mentioned two aspects which, strictly speaking, could attach to the issue of admissibility, but we agreed that that's not what we were going to concentrate upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay? Yes. I think Mr. Graham, and please explain to him that we haven't kept him waiting capriciously.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I just ask when the next break is going to be so I don't run through it. --.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm a bit lost because.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: A very good question because normally it would be in ten minutes' time. Ram, I think you have to work this out, please. I think you have to consult with the technical staff, interpreters, et cetera, because the break as such that we had a relatively short one, so you tell us when we shall have the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. With the indulgence of the rest of the staff, to whom I'm very grateful and thank you, next break will be at 4.15 and it will be a full break. Good afternoon to you, Mr. Graham.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal with which you are familiar. Prior to your testimony could you kindly make the solemn declaration which is required by our rules?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think I can avoid preliminaries. Mr. Nicholls, please make yourself comfortable. Mr. Nicholls will go first and then you will be cross-examined by the various Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Mr. Graham.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: As you know we are both speaking the same language, so let's try to have a little break between our questions and answers so that the interpreters can stay with us. Can you please give me your full name?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Alistair Paul Graham.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: 21st of May 1962.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And which country were you born in?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: In England.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I want to first quite briefly go through some of your background. What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: I'm a detective inspector with the Lancashire police which is a provincial force in England.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you run through for the Trial Chamber, please, your career from the beginning of joining the field of law enforcement, where you first worked as a policeman and the subsequent steps in your career?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: I joined the police, Lancashire police, in 1985 as a uniformed police officer. I moved in 1990 to become a detective constable. In 1991 I was promoted to the rank of detective Sergeant. I undertook a number of roles in that rank until January 1998 when I became a temporary detective inspector. In June 1998, I then joined the Tribunal as an investigator, assigned to the team that was investigating the crimes committed in and around Srebrenica in 1995. I remained in that role until 1999, I think it was August, when I became temporary and then the permanent head of mission in the ICTY's field office in Kosovo. I remained there until May 2001, when I returned to The Hague as an investigations team leader with responsibility initially just for the Srebrenica investigation and trial-related matters, but as the Tribunal started to downsize, I took on responsibility as team leader for other investigations and trial support issues. I remained in that role until October 2004 when I left the Tribunal, and I became a consultant investigator with the UN investigation into the oil-for-food based in New York. I remained with that, the inquiry committee there, until December 2005, when I returned to the U.K. to my home police force. I returned there as a detective sergeant, held a number of temporary roles, and then was promoted to substantive inspector earlier this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to jump now to -- right away to the reason you're here as a witness and to discuss the interviews you conducted with Mr. Borovcanin. I want to talk first about the first interview from 20th of February 2002. Can you explain briefly in your own words how that interview came about, how Mr. Borovcanin -- how Borovcanin was brought to the place where he was interviewed, the process by which he was notified of the interview?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: At that time there was a protocol in place whereby an official request was put through the requests unit here at the Tribunal. It went to a representative of the RS authorities, Mr. Jovicic, and it went through that way for the request to be made for people to be made available for interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to show you some documents now on e-court. The first is 02864, and I think it should be page 5. Now it may take a minute to appear but an image of a document should appear on the screen in front of you in a minute. And we are going to go -- need to go to page 5, which is ERN 06106273 in the English original. Thank you. Now, that's a little bit small. I can't -- are you able to read that on your screen?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. This is a summons dated 11 February 2002. It's fairly obvious, but can you just tell us what this is, this document?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: It's almost the pro forma that was used to go through the request unit to request the RS authorities to make somebody available, and this was the actual, the summons document, that we would ask to be passed to the relevant person.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we look at paragraph 3, is the summons to interview Mr. Borovcanin as a witness or as a suspect?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: To be questioned as a suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to now go to -- it should be the next page, page 6. This is also dated 11 February 2002. It's a Prosecutor's undertaking regarding Mr. Borovcanin. Can you just tell us what these documents are used for, or were used for at that time?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: It was really a confirmation of safe passage for whoever was being summonsed. The RS authorities felt it would assist people to come if they knew that they would have safe passage to and from an interview, and it was not entrapment to have them arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to now go to a different 65 ter number, 02865, page -- if we could have the translation as well in English. It's too small for me to tell if it's the correct -- that's correct. We need the English larger for Mr. Graham to be able to read it. This is a document with a number ICTY-2-TJ-213/02, a letter from Mr. Jovicic you referred to to the Ministry of Justice. Can you just explain to us, if you can, what this letter was for in relation to the summonses we have been talking about?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: I played no part in this particular part of the process, but I understood this to be the letter from Mr. Jovicic that went through to the Ministry of Justice in Republika Srpska to have the summonses delivered.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Next one I'd like to look at is P02864, at page 9, if we can have the English up there. Now, this is a document dated 20th of February 2002, with the same reference number as the previous document, from Mr. McCloskey -- to Mr. McCloskey from Mr. Jovicic, and very simply, was this standard to get these type of letters showing that summonses had been served and signed for?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Yes. This was a standard response.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if we can go to page 10 now, please, and if we could also have the English up, please? And again, fairly clear but this document dated the 18th of February 2002 is the receipt for the service of summons signed by Mr. Borovcanin; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Yes. It's definitely a signed receipt. I'm assuming it's his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm done with those documents now. Now, on the -- did Mr. Borovcanin -- well, did Mr. Borovcanin appear for his interview on the 20th of February 2002, in the morning?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: As best you recall, who did he come with, if anybody? Did he come by himself or with anybody?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: I don't actually recall seeing him with anybody when I first met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just to be clear, prior to that morning, had you ever met Mr. Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: No, I had not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And had you ever spoken to him?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: No, I had not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, before the interview started, did he say whether he was -- whether he would have an attorney for the interview?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: I don't know how the conversation came about. The assumption that I had was that an attorney would be there. It was definitely a conversation when I asked where the attorney was, and I was told he would be coming later. But the exact content of that conversation I can't remember after this length of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And who was present for the interview, and if you have any difficulty remembering the names of anybody, interpreter or something, I've got the transcript.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: For the first interview I recall Mr. Borovcanin was present, Mr. McCloskey, myself and the interpreter, who I think was Ms. Markovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And can you tell us, we will look at it a little later, but how did that interview begin?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: It began -- I would -- I began the interview by putting the tapes on and then going through the -- Mr. Borovcanin, his rights with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I was going to ask you, you've gone ahead which is good. How was the interview recorded, just very plainly if you can tell us what kinds of equipment it was and whether it was digital or -- you've already said it was taped?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: It was a tape recorder with a small microphone that stood on the table.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. What I'd like to do now, Your Honours, is play the very beginning of the interview of 20th of February 2002. It's a segment of approximately ten minutes, which is essentially the introduction and the -- Mr. Graham advising Mr. Borovcanin of his rights?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it going to show anything which is different from what we can read out from the transcript? Because our decision was very clear. I have it here. We had restricted -- basically you will -- what we decided was that as long as what you wished to play is already reflected in the transcripts, there is no need for you to play it. But if there is anything that goes beyond what we can perceive through -- from reading the transcript, then you are of course allowed to make use of the video recording. That was the understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, the only point it adds is to the transcript. The transcript is accurate and our friends have helped us make some corrections late last night to a couple words. What it does add only is hearing the clarity in the way people are speaking, the tone of voice, how long there are between questions and answers, and any lag that there might be or lack thereof. The issue is the -- how Mr. Borovcanin was advised of his rights and how clearly and well it was done, and I just thought you can actually hear how it was done. I was only going to play this first segment, but it is possible to see the words, the exact words, on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but, yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, but I've been given, and I think the rest of the Defence teams, 16 pages of items from the transcripts that go to the issue, and when Your Honour mentions at page 27, line 21 and 22, when you say we decided that as long as what you wish to play is already reflected in the transcripts, there is no need to play it, I guess my question is do you also -- does the Bench also have these 16 pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. He can ask me. I have not passed those out yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The position, as I see it, you wish to speak, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour, I was trying to object, but Mr. Meek was faster than myself. Basically, I understood Trial Chamber's ruling precisely just like you put it straight away to Mr. Nicholls. I mean, there is absolutely no difference between what's on the tape with these transcript. Furthermore this transcript is a bit more accurate because it does indicate that a certain portion was not translated to Mr. Borovcanin, and we have absolutely no dispute with the Prosecution that that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Our decision, Mr. Nicholls, was very categoric. We had stated that with one exception, we do not see any need for the playing of the tape in whole or in part at this stage with respect to the question of admissibility. The only exception that we granted would be where the Prosecution can establish that the playing of a portion of the tape is directly relevant to the question of admissibility, and the point that would be demonstrated is not apparent from the transcript itself. Now, you're jumping the gun because basically if later on Mr. Lazarevic or others will question the proprietness or the -- and adequacy of the caution that was done in the beginning, then the question may arise whether you should make use of any excerpts at all. But short of that, I don't think you should embark on trying to explain to us what happened in the beginning of the -- if we can perceive that by reading the transcript itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. I apologise. I might not have had the order completely clear, as I should have. We can proceed just with using the transcript, and I would then now pass out to you if I can portions of the transcript I'm going to go over with Mr. Graham. It can also be viewed on e-court, but these hard copies may be easier to begin with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. I hope it has been understood that the idea is very limited use of the tape. It applies to you, it applies also to the Defence to an extent and then obviously, if questions are asked which highlight certain discrepancies that can be clarified by use of the tape or excerpts thereof, we will discuss that but not for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, if I can now just then pass out to you these excerpts from the transcript of -- which are from both the 2002 February and March interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead Mr. Nicholls, please. First of all, can I ask you how long you think your examination-in-chief will last?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think less than an hour. I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead. I'm asking you because in the information that we got from the registrar, it's 15 hours. And I was wondering whether there was a mistake there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think that's when we were all going to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not from the registrar. It's from our staff, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's when we were all going to listen to the tape for several days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought so. I just wanted to make sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And maybe if we can just have these pages up on e-court as well, it might be good. This is 2852, I believe, starting with page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, first of all, Mr. Graham, just to be clear, while you were here over the weekend, you reviewed this -- the transcript of your interviews with Mr. Borovcanin; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recognise the document you have right before you now from the 20th of February 2002?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And what I want you to do first, if you can, is just read through the first three pages, up to line -- just the first three pages, and tell me if, to the best of your recollection, and the best of your memory, this is an accurate transcript of what took place at the beginning of the interview?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Do you want me to read it out loud?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. Just to yourself. Could I just say one thing to Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You will notice on page 2, at line 13, against you is underlined and then we have NTTLJB. That signifies that on listening to the audio, that part of the English was not translated to Mr. Borovcanin. So he would have heard that in English but not in his language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for pointing that out, Mr. Nicholls. Could I ask when that was established?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That was established at about 10.30 p.m. last night by my friends who e-mailed me and advised me, and I had the transcript corrected. And I won't speak for my friends, but I believe we've both looked at this transcript quite a bit and agree that it's as accurate as it can be and it's at present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The interview was conducted in which language?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In English, Your Honour, with an interpreter who was interpreting the questions asked in English into the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. I would imagine so but just for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And it was -- there was simultaneous translation there and then?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And how have you been able to establish, for example, that on the same page, "u redu" was not translated into English and the words "against you" in English were not translated into Serb or Croat?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: By listening, by having people who speak both languages listen carefully to the tape recordings, to the audio recordings and our friends have pointed out errors, and we ourselves have reviewed the tape and tried to catch as many mistakes and all the mistakes that we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not trying to do what Mr. Meek would call go through the back door but if were you to hear the first ten minutes, it gives you a very good idea of just how this interview went.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We wouldn't be able to establish that these two words were not translated into Serb or Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what's the point? Let's go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Have you reviewed those first three pages, Mr. Graham?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And the best you remember, does this accurately reflect your advising Mr. Borovcanin of his rights?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, while you were advising Mr. Borovcanin of these rights, if you remember, were you reading from something or going off your memory of what Rule 42 requires or a mixture? Can you explain how you provided these rights to Mr. Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: I had an aide-memoire, a piece of paper on the desk next to me. Some of it I was reading verbatim, other parts I was using as a reminder to make sure that I covered all the issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did Mr. Borovcanin comment on the summons in any way?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Yes, he pointed out to me that he'd read it, and his forename was wrong on the summons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Were you aware or did he tell you what his profession, what his job was, at the time of the interview?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: As I recall he told me he was a Professor at the police academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, just describe as best you can, you remember what -- what the atmosphere was during while were you beginning this interview and reading Mr. Borovcanin his rights, and what his demeanour was? I know you can't say what he was thinking or feeling, but how did the whole beginning of the interview seem to you?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: It started the way most interviews started, formally. But everybody in the room became more relaxed as time went on, and we settled into the environment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to look at page 2, line 8, where it states that the question you asked was or what you told Mr. Borovcanin was, "Now, based on the information that the Tribunal has, the Prosecutor believes that you may be a suspect who is responsible for committing acts which may be chargeable under the Tribunal statute." Can you tell us if you remember, if you can explain, why you used the phrase "you may be a suspect"? How you came about that description?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: That is a verbatim quote from the aide-memoire that I had been given when I returned to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And then was that something standard you used in suspect interviews or was this any different in this interview?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: No. That is something standard that I used in very many interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: During this interview, at any time -- let me ask it this way: Was this the only time that you advised Mr. Borovcanin of his rights?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: No. I believe I advised him of his rights a number of times during the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And when did you, best as you remember, when did you do that or how did you decide when you would again advise him of his rights?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: If there was a break of more than a couple of minutes; for example, if I were just turning a tape over, I would not look to readvise of rights. But if we have a coffee break or if we broke for lunch, my protocol was to remind the person who was being interviewed of their rights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we have a reference to such like portions from the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For ease of reference later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And in that case, whether you have also, if the language used, terminology used, is identical and anything you do say will be recorded and could be used in evidence against you in a later Tribunal proceedings, including trial, whether in these later instances, the words against you, if used, were translated into Serbo-Croat, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. They are not all in the excerpt I passed out, but what I propose to do is briefly go through the different times during the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't want to interrupt you, but I think this -- these could become relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's where I was going, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we could go to page 23, please of the same, that is not in your packet, I'll have to do this in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I again, after talking to my learned colleagues, I believe that these 16 pages that were hand -- given us in hard copy are what had been scanned in e-court. I just want to know has -- have these interviews been scanned into e-court and released in their entirety?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. That's the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I object. We had a conversation this morning, not only with Mr. Nicholls, with Mr. McCloskey, that because this is a two-step process, and you may very well decide that if it's admissible at all, it's only admissible against the person being interviewed, Mr. Borovcanin, and that you may very well delete or redact other names. And now apparently the Prosecution has gone ahead and put into e-court the entire transcripts without any redactions before you've ever made a ruling, and I object to it. I don't think it's proper, and they agreed that they were not going to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls? Do you wish to comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yeah. Frankly I don't understand the objection at all. Your Honours ruling again was that we can make use of these transcripts during this hearing. That's when I asked -- Mr. McCloskey would like to address you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, let's finish the Prosecution and then you give --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: My understanding was that I was not going to put these documents into e-court and distribute them until they were going to be used. Now, I've decided now to go through the different areas of the transcript, I'm going to limit it to where the portions relevant to this hearing, which are primarily where Mr. Borovcanin is advised of his rights. And that's the pages which I will call up on e-court. And I don't see anything wrong with that. The other option is I can pass out whole hard copies to everybody, but that's not -- e-court is so that we avoid that. And I honestly don't understand where Mr. Meek is coming from with this because he did ask earlier that we not put everything out, and we agreed to that until we knew we were going to use them; and we are going to use them now for the limited basis of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. I think this is a useless discussion, a futile discussion, Mr. Meek, because we have already decided that, without prejudice to the issue of redactions to be dealt with in due course, for the purpose of this stage, namely the debate evidence and debate on admissibility, both the tape and the transcript will be marked for identification. So how do you expect them to be marked for identification and not be in e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, with all due respect, all due respect, I thought the ruling was that the use of the transcripts would be for the limited purpose of whether or not this statement is admissible. Now, there are portions of it, there are 16 pages here, that may go to that issue. And now he's going to put in 300 pages which goes far beyond, far beyond, the issues in this hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you have missed the whole -- so I'm not using -- I'm not trying to use language which is in any way offensive, but what I mean to tell you is that there is -- obviously we are not on the same wave length on this because our position was as follows: Possible redactions insofar as they may become necessary, within the ambit of the decision that we will later need to take in relation to the admissibility is one thing. All rights are reserved and continue to be reserved for that purpose. But in the meantime, both the tapes and the transcripts, we decided to mark for identification because it makes no sense not having them introduced in the system and marked for identification if we need to proceed with a serious examination-in-chief and cross-examination of this witness in relation to the admissibility aspect. Now, which parts of the tape, transcripts you make use of is your own business. I can assure you that we are not going to spend our time reading through what is or may not be necessary to read if that is your concern. But the matter of redactions or possible redactions is none of our concern for the time being. It will become important or may become important later on depending on what decision we will come to but, which of course we don't know for the time being, but that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And frankly I feel like Alice in Wonderland, I've fallen down the rabbit hole again. What you're say is that the Prosecution can use what they want to use or what they feel is necessary for this hearing. So frankly, if they say we think the whole 15 hours is necessary, then I guess they get to play the whole 15 hours of tapes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again we are not on the same wave length.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Apparently not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you will know quite well that we are not. Okay. We'll have a break now. Maybe you can thrash this out with the Prosecution. 25 minutes break and then I'm very confident that we'll finish with your testimony by the end of tomorrow --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- Mr. Graham. We'll do our utmost. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls. The understanding is that you will proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Before we go to the next time you advised Mr. Borovcanin of his rights, let me go back for a minute to the beginning of the interview. We don't need to bring them up again, but this is referenced on pages 2 and 3 of the transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, sorry to interrupt you but I don't know whether we'll finish today or tomorrow, but one thing I certainly don't want to forget is to publicly announce that we are scheduled to resume our sittings after the recess on the 20th of August, that's a Monday. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: (redacted), and we were scheduled to sit in the morning, they were scheduled to sit in the afternoon, and they have asked us to consider not sitting on that day so that they can have the entire day for this witness. We have acceded to that. The quid pro quo, however, is that on the 22nd, that's Wednesday, instead of having only the morning sitting, as scheduled, we will have a whole day; in other words what we will miss on Monday we will make good for on Wednesday. So I'm announcing that so that you will know that we will not be starting on the 20th as scheduled, but be prepared for a long day on the 22nd, or a longer day on the 22nd. Yes, sorry to have interrupted you like this, but I know that I would have probably forgot it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Since my attention is being drawn since we don't know whether that person is a protected witness or not, we will redact from the transcript any reference to who he is, in other words, his position, all right? Thank you. Let's proceed and again my apologies for the interruption, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could we go back to page -- well, we don't need to go back. Let me just ask you this, Witness: Drawing your attention now to the beginning of the interview at 9.02 a.m. on the 20th, you told us and we can see in the transcript, that Mr. Borovcanin's attorney was not with him, and you stated as it says in the transcript, "Mr. Borovcanin said that his attorney would be joining them, joining you, later in the day." Can you just tell us briefly, and it's in the transcript but, what did you and Mr. McCloskey say to Mr. Borovcanin about the fact that he didn't have a lawyer with him at that point; although, he was willing to continue the interview. Just tell us about that discussion about his options for having his lawyer come or stopping the interview?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, Mr. Borovcanin had pointed that out to me before we went into interview and said he wanted to continue. I was mindful of that fact, and I wanted to make sure that it was on the record. So I made a point of stressing the fact that we didn't need to start without the lawyer present, and we could stop at any stage if Mr. Borovcanin wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And did Mr. McCloskey also talk about Mr. Borovcanin's right to stop the interview or suspend the interview?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He reiterated the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And Mr. Borovcanin agreed to continue without his attorney at that point; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, we've got page 23 of the transcript, that is page 21 in the B/C/S if it's needed. Just refresh your memory by looking at that page. That is on the screen in front of you. It would not be with you in hard copy for the moment. Have you read that to yourself?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just very briefly, is that accurate from your memory that after the first break, at 10.42, when you continued, you again advised Mr. Borovcanin that he had the right not say anything, to remain silent, that anything he said would be recorded and used in evidence, and that he had of course the right to stop and wait for his lawyer to arrive and then to decide what to do next?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Yes, it is. I was reminding him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And we can see at line 19, you asked him can I confirm that you're still happy to continue without legal presentation at this time, and his answer was yes?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Without legal representation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to now go to page 43 of this document. That's page 40, I believe, in the B/C/S. And can you just read page 43 to yourself, and then I'll ask for you to read page 44 to yourself. Tell me when you've read 43 and we can go to 44.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: I'm ready for 44.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And could we have, I'm sorry, a little bit more of the English version so that I can see the lines that are -- well, in any event, we are now the time 1406 in the interview, and it's stated on the previous page, this is after about a two hour lunch break and during that time, Mr. Borovcanin had met with his lawyer; is that right? Is that conform to your recollection?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And am I correct that as soon as Mr. Borovcanin's lawyer arrived, a break was taken of two hours?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: I can't remember if we were taking the break, and the lawyer turned up during the break or we broke -- I think a note was put under the door, if I remember correctly, saying that Mr. Borovcanin's lawyer had arrived and for that reason we stopped the tape immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, for your reference that is on page 42 that Mr. Graham is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, again, you've read through this. At this stage, after Mr. Borovcanin's counsel has arrived, we see here that you have again advised him of his rights even though as -- now with his lawyer present; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And Your Honours I would just draw your attention again that the interpreter made the same error on line 6 of page 44 and failed to translate "against you" into Mr. Borovcanin's language. And I think we can see here it's obvious Mr. Borovcanin again agreed to continue with the interview. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls I notice that this is the second time that, as you put it, same mistake was made by the interpreter. Have you tried to verify whether there was a reason for omitting the translation of the words "against you" into B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand Your Honour completely. I think it was just an error in the translation, and we'll see later on she makes a reverse -- she makes a mistake sort of in the reverse, later on, the question is "you may be a suspect" and she translates as "you are a suspect," so I don't know the reason. Later on in the interview, it is -- we'll get to it, it's correctly translated, so I believe it's just a slip of the tongue. And there were several errors which -- and we've caught as many as we can in this transcript including those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I asked you the question because in my mind, I wanted to know whether it would perhaps be superfluous for someone who is translating into B/C/S to specifically translate those words too. The reason is in some jurisdictions, for example, giving the caution you don't use the words "against you".

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's right. And of course, under our rule they are not required, they are not in our rule either, but I can't say I know what the reason was that the interpreter missed those two words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fair enough. I don't want to hear more. I think that's enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, let me -- before we go on, and I'll look at another couple pages, you talked about how the interview started. As the interview continued can you just describe the atmosphere during the interview, and the way people conducted themselves?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: I have no recollection, but it certainly didn't stand out in my mind that there was any problem or any tension.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And was there any joking around by anybody present, any humour?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: On several occasions, Mr. Borovcanin made a joke. I think he asked at least one occasion if he could make a joke.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to go to page 90 now of this interview, if we may, and that's page 83 in the B/C/S. This is in the packet that I handed out, Your Honours. I just want to draw your attention, Mr. Graham, to lines 19 to 20.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, this is towards the end of the interview. I just want to confirm that as per the rules you gave Mr. Borovcanin the chance to say anything he wished to say at the end of the interview?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to look at page 91 now, which should be page 84 in the B/C/S. I'd like you to read that whole page to yourself.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. And again to confirm that matches your memory of your questioning at the end of Mr. Borovcanin, that at line 2 you asked him if he was happy that he'd asked the questions of his own free will, and he stated that he had. At line 5 you asked him, "you've not been threatened promised or induced to give any of the answers you've given today?" And then he said, "Except for some threatening looks, there was nothing else. I'm just joking." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: I remember the line, one or two of those lines in particular, but this is the standard end that I would do on a tape-recorded interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And again, he confirmed that in his words, when you asked him if he had any complaints about the way he'd been treated before and during the interview that everything was correct, and then he made another little joke about drinking too much coffee, right?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: That's right. It's the coffee line that I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And just to be clear, that's the interview -- the end of the first interview in February 2002?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just to be very clear, from the time that Mr. Borovcanin's attorney appeared at 11.59 and there was a note slipped under the door saying he was there, from the transcript we see that to the end of the interview he was present. Was there any time he was not present during the interview with Mr. Borovcanin after he'd arrived?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Not while the interview was being undertaken, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to now move on quickly to the second interview you did with Mr. Borovcanin which began on the 20th of February 2002. Sorry, the 11th of March, 2002. I don't want to take the time to go through the same chain of documents, but can you confirm to us that similarly he was issued with a summons through the RS authorities. He was given a Prosecutor's undertaking not to arrest him and that he signed a receipt for that summons and appeared for the interview?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: That is my understanding, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And again, that was a summons to appear as a suspect for an interview?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This should now be -- if we could have 2853 in e-court, please, page 1? Sorry, just before we get to that, do you remember if you gave Mr. Borovcanin a copy of the audiotapes of the first interview, and if you did, when you did that, approximately?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: I don't believe I gave him a copy of the interview when it first finished because it was a single tape recording machine. I came back to The Hague, and I believe it was on this next visit that I provided the tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: I may be mistaken on that. It may have gone through on an actual-- through Mr. Jovicic, but I can't remember. But I definitely did not provide them at the end of the first is interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'll try to do this quite quickly, but if you could -- you've got them in front of you, if you could please read pages 1 to 3 of the 11 March interview. All right. And you can stop at line 6 on page 3 because that's the only part we are interested in is up to there.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: I've read up to that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now if you can just confirm as far as you remember this is an accurate transcript of the interview?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And now, at this second interview, Mr. Borovcanin's counsel was there from the very beginning?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And again, you have gone through the rights to be given to a suspect?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Yes, I'll have been using the same aide-memoire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours on page 2 if we can have at line 17, here, Mr. Graham, as he has before, says, "Anything that you do say will be recorded and could be used in evidence against you in a later Tribunal proceeding." And I had a B/C/S speaker just before court today check and that was correctly translated on this occasion. Nobody made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The same questions really: Can you describe Mr. Borovcanin's demeanour during this second interview, and the general feeling from your perspective in the room during the interview; how it was conducted and how people felt?
