utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: I can't fully recollect how it was in the room, but there is -- nothing comes back that there was any tension or any problems. It was a typical interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And I'm sorry I should have said this at the beginning, just to be clear on who was present at this interview, it's all the same people except that Mr. Borovcanin's attorney is there the entire time, and the interpreter is a different person, we can see on page 1 at line 11; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, again, do you recall whether you advised Mr. -- whether you followed that practice and advised Mr. Borovcanin of his rights after breaks had taken place during the interview? Did you do that again in this interview as well?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection I did after every substantial break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to look at pages 49 to 50 of this interview, the second interview. Page 49 is page 46 in the B/C/S. And that should come up on the screen for you. And on page 50, I'm only interested up to line 10, the end of line 10. And we can go to page 50 now, please. And I'll give you a chance to read down to line 10 on the English, if we can scroll that over a bit. You can't see the lines but line 10 is where Mr. Borovcanin says, "yes," and then it goes to a large long question by you.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Yes, I've read that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Again, does this conform to your advising Mr. Borovcanin of his rights after the lunch break?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Yes, it's what I will have said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And we can see here that you've at lines 5 and 6 you've slightly changed the phrases you use and say, "And the other thing that I need to remind you is that because you're being interviewed as a suspect, you do not have to say anything or answer any of our questions unless you wish to do so." And then you go on. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: I believe it will be. It -- there was no reason for not saying exactly the same words as last time. I was using the same aide-memoire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But my point is here is here we have you will be interviewed as a as a suspect not may be a suspect?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, I notice that once more, the words "against you" supposedly were not translated into Serbo-Croat. Do I take it that now it's a different interpreter still? Or have we reverted to the first interpreter, the one that was present during the first interview?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. We're --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm asking the question because I wish to establish that both, whether both interpreters actually made the same mistake, as you put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct, Your Honour, you're correct, Your Honour, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I won't go through it, but again at pages 73 and at pages 91 you just briefly remind Mr. Borovcanin of his rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: For Your Honours, we don't need to go through that in detail. I'd like to go to page 111 of this interview now, please. That's page 101 of the B/C/S, I believe. Wait a second. I might have the wrong page. Sorry, you can take that off. I'm sorry, it is page 111.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm only concerned with the very last line, page 25. We are now getting towards the end of the interview. The part I'm interested in is Peter McCloskey says, "We will be finished. Do you have any questions, any concerns, right now?" And Mr. Borovcanin on the next page makes a joke. And if we could go to page 113 now, which is 102 in the B/C/S, and I'm interested in lines 22 to 26. So can you just tell me when you've read the bottom section of that?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: I have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. And again there, can we look at page 114 now? Next page. And then just very briefly there, again, as we've seen before you've confirmed with Mr. Borovcanin that he's happy with the way the interview has been conducted, and he states that the answers have been given of his own free will and without inducements, threats, or promises; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Can we go now to the bottom of page 114, if we could scroll down, we see there that's correct, that the interview continued the next day at 9.16 on the 12th of March?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if we go to 115 now, please, which is 104 in the B/C/S? We can see there at the top of the page that the same people are present at the interview including Mr. Borovcanin's attorney; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And again we don't need to go through it, if you could just read this page to yourself. And then can you just confirm that again during the continuation of this same interview on the next day, at the beginning of the day, you advised Mr. Borovcanin of his rights as we see here on the paper?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, if I could just again draw your attention to the fact that in line 20, "Against you" was not translated into Mr. Borovcanin's language. However, another mistake at line 16, when Mr. Graham told Mr. Borovcanin that, "the Tribunal believes you may be a suspect," that was translated to him in his language as "you have the status of a suspect." And if we could go now just to the very end of this interview, page 162, lines I'm interested in on page 162 are lines 3 to 6. Can you just read those to yourself. And here you've again given at the end of the interview Mr. Borovcanin the opportunity to clarify anything he thinks there might be some confusion over. You say,"Now is the time to do that, if there is anything he wants to add," correct?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And now if we can go to the next page, please, page 163 which is also in the packet I've handed out, that's page 141 in the English, 141 in the B/C/S, if you could just read that whole page to yourself? Have you had a chance to read through that last page?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just to be clear, this is the end of your -- complete end of your second interview with Mr. Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And again, we don't need to go through it but at lines 13 through 17, on page 163, you again confirm that Mr. Borovcanin is happy with the way the interview has been conducted, and he's given the answers of his own free will. I won't read the whole thing. At line 15, Mr. Borovcanin makes another joke, "I'm really happy I lost four kilos in two days." And at line 17, after being asked if he has any complaints, he says, "No, everything was okay." Is that --

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: From rereading the transcript, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. Could I have one moment, Your Honours? I'm just about done. I just want to check something.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think at this time I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Now, in our ruling we also established that it will be the Borovcanin team who will go first. So Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Graham. My name is Aleksandar Lazarevic and together with my colleagues in my team, I appear here for Mr. Ljubomir Borovcanin before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, we will have a break at 6.20.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for this information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is a suggestion on our part so that we don't possibly don't break your cross-examination, Mr. Lazarevic, but I need the consensus of everyone, particularly the persons behind the glass screens, if we could have a 15 minute break now and then when we resume, we continue right up to 7.00?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, as for Mr. Borovcanin's Defence position, we are fine with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it will be helpful because you won't have to interrupt your cross-examination, but I want to make sure that it is acceptable to the rest of the staff.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It is for interpreters, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is for interpreters and for the technicians and recorders? Okay. All right. So we'll have 15 minutes now. We will resume at roughly quarter to 6.00 or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: M. Lazarevic, s'il vous plait.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Graham, before the break, I just introduced myself and the members of my team. I just want to make sure you understand that I am the Defence counsel for Mr. Borovcanin. I listened very carefully to my learned friend from the Prosecution and before that I had occasion to review your career background. There is just one detail that I would like to clarify. Do you have a degree in law?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. When you began to work for the Office of the Prosecutor at the ICTY here in The Hague, did you complete a specialised training course for the job that you were to perform in the OTP?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to speak to your colleagues who were working on similar jobs? Did they maybe instruct you as to whether your job was perhaps different to the one you had in Lancashire?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: I did a lot of background, and I spoke to people that were working at the Tribunal when I made an application. So I knew exactly what I was applying for and what my role would be, but I was an experienced detective officer back in Lancashire at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Of course, I'm not questioning your experience at all. I just wanted to establish whether you were given some special instructions from your colleagues here regarding procedural differences between that job and the one you had before.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: There was an induction course that gave an outline, but when I joined, my initial role was involved in attending exhumation sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I have just one more question on this subject, and then I will move on to more specific ones regarding the interview with Mr. Borovcanin. During the time you worked for the Office of the Prosecutor at the ICTY, did you have occasion to familiarise yourself with the legislation of the countries that came into being after the break-up of the former Yugoslavia; namely, the legislation governing pre-criminal and criminal proceedings?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Not to my recollection, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me now move on to the interviews with Mr. Borovcanin. I suppose before you came to testify, and this seems to be confirmed by the chief examination by my colleague, Mr. Nicholls, you had occasion to review these interviews in detail?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: The first opportunity I had to actually read a version of the transcript was on my flight over. I was actually attending a training course up until Friday, and I flew on the Saturday so that was the first opportunity I had was to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps also listen to the audio tapes, or did you just look at the transcript?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Just the transcript. I've heard segments of the audiotape over the last two days, but I've certainly not heard them right the way through.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Did that help you remember any details of those interviews with Mr. Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Both by reading and listening to the segments I did, yes, it did jog my memory on certain things.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: But apart from that, you did not have any independent recollection of that interview?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Same here. Maybe you can rephrase it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I will rephrase it, then, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before reading the transcripts and listening to segments of the audiotapes, how would you qualify your recollection of your interviews with Mr. Borovcanin? What kind of memory of them did you have?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: I believe I had a good memory. It was a significant interview. I didn't do a huge number of interviews while I was in the Tribunal. Being a team leader, it was a selected number, but I certainly remembered that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have answered my question. Before these interviews with Mr. Borovcanin were scheduled and before they took place, did you undertake any special preparations for them within the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Not beyond background reading and preparations, so I knew what matters would be discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have already had an opportunity during the

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Borovcanin. They contain a notification to the effect that Mr. Borovcanin, in the capacity of a suspect, is to show up at a certain place and time regarding an interview. Is that what we could say about these summons?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Well, is it a summons asking him to attend, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And as we had occasion to see, the summons is addressed through the liaison officer to the Ministry of Justice of the country whose national the interviewee is, but ultimately the summons is delivered to the person concerned by the Ministry of the Interior; that is the police. Did I describe the procedure correctly?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: I wouldn't -- don't think I'm in a position to state how it was actually delivered, but the intention was that it would be delivered to the person named on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Of course, I can't insist if you are not very familiar with that procedure, but my question was who was actually responsible for handing the summons to the person. But if you can't assist me with that, I'll move on. We have just seen the summons. Would you agree with me that the summons addressed to the person does not contain the qualification or the name or the act that the person is suspected of having committed, nor the relevant article in the statute, nor any mention of the rights the person has?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Can I see a copy to refresh my memory?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think we need to see the English version would be the one. That's ERN number 06106273. And then 6274 I don't think is relevant for this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And can I just say for the record that's 02864 is our number.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Page 5, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then perhaps also relevant for your question is the letter written by Trifun Jovicic to the Ministry of Republika Srpska personally to Biljana Maric, minister, and that would be 2865. Yes, 2865. I think those are the two that you need to see for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just that I think my friend was asking for the summons, not the undertaking, and that's not what we have on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. The summons is -- no, no. What you need to see on the screen for the time being is the one, the document signed by Graham Blewitt dated 11 February 2002, which is P02864. What we have there is the other one, 2865.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe it should be page 5, if I was following properly what -- the document is P02864, page 5. This is the summons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What you see on the screen is the right document, isn't it? Is that correct, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So that's -- do you have it in front of you, Mr. Graham.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So your question again, please, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: By all means, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the question basically is whether there is any reference to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's been a while before we were able to get the document on the screen, so it's perhaps a good idea to repeat the question. From the summons you see before you, would you agree with me that it is not emphasised in the summons which acts the person is charged with, the article of the Statute referring to that act is not quoted, and the rights enjoyed by that person in keeping with the rules are not mentioned either?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Obviously I've not worked with these rules since I left the Tribunal in 2004 but the question stated the acts the person is charged with, the person isn't charged with acts prior to going for the interview. I don't have the definition of suspect, but I think it's may be charged or may be chargeable under the Tribunal statute. But with relation to this document, it was a standard OTP document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just to clear this up, according to our rules, Rule 2, which deals with definitions, "suspect" is "a person concerning whom the Prosecution, Prosecutor, possesses reliable information which tends to show that the person may have committed a crime over which the Tribunal has jurisdiction." But I don't know whether it's a question of interpretation or not, but your question was translated into English as if to mean, emphasising which acts the person is charged with. There is no charge at the time. If he is a suspect he's only a suspect. But I don't know whether it's important or not for the purpose of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour -- [In English] It's not relevant, but let's be precise about this. I was just trying to establish what is the content of the summons itself, that three of these, well, warnings and statutes -- and situation with the statutes and of course that the suspect person does not understand from the summons itself what is the name of the -- well, maybe I should not give evidence. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so, yes. I think so. Yes, go ahead with your next question, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Graham, would you agree with me if I said that the person who has the status of suspect has the right not to talk to you at all and to refuse talking to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Yes, they have.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you agree that this right that you agree the suspect had is not clearly stated in the summons?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: We are getting into a legal argument which I believe is outside my remit as to the summons for attending and actually talking or not answering questions when you actually answer to the summons, but I'm not a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I quite accept that we should not be discussing the legal aspect of this, but do you see any mention of anything like that in this summons, something to the effect of, "You have the right of not responding to this invitation from the Office of the Prosecutor"?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Well, those are, excuse me, Your Honours, those are different questions and it's sort of apples and oranges. There is a question about the right to respond to the summons and to appear for the interview and that's a different question from whether you need to speak or answer questions. So I think maybe he needs to break that down a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Definitely. Mr. Lazarevic, please don't mix the two together as if they were the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe that it was the issue of interpretation but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I accept that without reservation, but what you are obviously referring to is you're just asking the witness to confirm that in the summons itself there is no indication as to the suspect's rights regarding the interview. That's what you meant, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Precisely so, what this witness can see on the screen, just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And what he can see is what we can see. So I would suggest that you proceed with your next question. There isn't anything such as suspect's rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The first interview between the OTP and Mr. Borovcanin took place on the 20th of February 2002, and according to my information and the transcript, it began at 9.02 a.m., didn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: I don't have the transcript in front of me, but I think that's the start time that's on it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [In English] Well, I can assure you that my colleagues from the Prosecution can follow this, and if they have any objection they will react promptly. [Interpretation] In the course of the cross-examination -- examination-in-chief led by Mr. Nicholls, you had occasion to see the relevant portions of the transcript regarding cautions given to Mr. Borovcanin regarding his status. Do you remember that, it was perhaps 40 minutes ago?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if you remember that portion of the transcript, when you gave that first caution to Mr. Borovcanin, you did not tell him that he does not have to talk to you at all, that he is free to leave the room; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: To answer questions that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Again I think for that type of question, it's fair to let the witness have a copy of the transcript in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Could the witness see page 2 of the first transcript, please, that I'm referring to page 2 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It's page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Page 2 of the English version, but I can't tell you which page is the B/C/S corresponding page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe it's also page 2 on B/C/S, but could be page 3, but I will just make sure when we see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If my friend thinks it will help, I've got a hard copy in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By all means, if there is no objection we can proceed that way; although, I can see it on the screen now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I just thought it might speed things up. He can start reading before waiting for the screen but it doesn't...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic. I think we can proceed with what we have there. It's sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then hand the hard copies to Mr. Graham, just make sure that the Defence are shown what he's being handed for formalities' sake.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you just repeat your question, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It wasn't my question, it was Mr. Lazarevic's question, but -- yes, and if you remember that portion of the transcript, when you gave that first caution to Mr. Borovcanin, you did not tell him that he does not have to talk to you at all, that he's free to leave the room; is that correct? That was Mr. Lazarevic's question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told him you didn't have to say or answer or say anything or answer our questions unless you want to do so. I did not tell him that he was free to leave the room. That as a given.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much, because that is in fact the gist I wanted to hear from you in response. One brief question: Do you speak the Bosnian Croat Serbian language as it is referred to here in the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you understand that language although you cannot speak it?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: No more than two or three words.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I apologise for objecting. It's just my friend just said "u redu" very well which reminded me -- sorry, on the page we have before us there are a couple of places in this transcript where it says, "u redu." It's not in B/C/S because that was not translated into English, and I just wanted to inform Your Honours of that, and I think that my friends agree that that means "okay," "all right," "very well."

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, I agreed upon this during the break with Mr. Nicholls, and there is no problem with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's move.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We see on the screen before us now the caution you made to Mr. Borovcanin, and we also see what Mr. Borovcanin heard in the language that he understands. Can we agree that Mr. Borovcanin did not hear the words "against you"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does he have to answer that question? It's already stipulated by --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If it is stipulated then I'm fine with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so. I have no doubt in my mind. Judge Kwon? Okay, go ahead. Next question, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In this caution you made to Mr. Borovcanin, on two occasions, you said, that there is a possibility that he is or may be a suspect. You used the words "you may be a suspect." [In English] "You are considered a possible suspect." [Interpretation] I'm drawing your attention precisely to these two expressions in this portion of the transcript. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: I agree I used the words "you may be a suspect," and I used the words "possible suspect" not "possibly a suspect," but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Of course, it doesn't change much to my question, but based on these words that you used, and I'm now not asking you this as a legal expert, does that mean, and do you accept that it can mean, that Mr. Borovcanin was not a suspect but could become one?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: That is certainly not the way it was intended and not the inflection that was in my voice when I said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you believe that Mr. Borovcanin would have been able to hear such distinctions in your English?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Mr. Borovcanin would have been listening to the interpreter and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Precisely. During examination-in-chief, you said that this caution that you repeated on many occasions during the interviews was a caution that was given to you ready made, that you were instructed to make to the interviewee, if I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: When I returned to the Tribunal as an investigations team leader and was aware I would be undertaking such interviews, I asked if there was an aide-memoire and this is what I was provided with by one of the investigators of the team that I then joined.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If I understood your evidence correctly, you continued to use that aide-memoire throughout the interviews with Mr. Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you use that aide-memoire every time you made that caution to Mr. Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, I did. I certainly had it on the table next to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And if I now accepted this answer of yours as reliable, that would mean that every further caution you made to Mr. Borovcanin would have been identical to the first one, correct?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: With the exception of possibly the odd word but...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Right. From your caution that we have on the transcript in front of us right now, I notice that you did not tell Mr. Borovcanin which act he may be suspected of having committed. You only said, "acts that may be punishable under the Statute of the Tribunal."

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: I said, "responsible for committing acts which may be chargeable under the Tribunal's statute."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Do you have any reason to believe that Mr. Borovcanin was familiar at the time with all the acts chargeable under the Statute of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: I think that's a misinterpretation of acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [In English] Let's take a look. Crimes may be, instead of acts, should be crimes.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't know if that was a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will rephrase and try to clarify. Do you have any reason to believe that at that moment, Mr. Borovcanin knew about all the criminal acts, such as genocide, crimes against humanity, violations of the Geneva Conventions and so on and so forth, that were envisaged by the Statute of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But you certainly know that there is a large number of criminal acts envisaged by the Statute of the Tribunal, and they are all different in terms of gravity and significance?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Yes, if we are talking about -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And not for a moment did you mention to Mr. Borovcanin the possibility that he could be suspected of having committed genocide or having conspired to commit genocide?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: No, it's not mentioned on the interview at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think you have anticipated my next question, but just to give a full picture to the Trial Chamber. Throughout these three interviews, the word "genocide" or "conspiracy to commit genocide" was never mentioned; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Not to the best of my recollection, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. Similarly, when the interview with Mr. Borovcanin commenced, when you cautioned him about his rights, not a word was said to describe the actions that Mr. Borovcanin may have committed that could have elements of a criminal act; in other words, not a word was said about what he was supposed to have done?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: No, but it wouldn't be at this stage because I was giving him his rights, not the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But throughout the interviews, from the very first one, through the second one and until the very end, there was not a single point when you told Mr. Borovcanin, "Look, we believe that you committed such and such an act," is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: I don't recall that being put as a direct question during the interviews, but the purpose of the interview was to establish where Mr. Borovcanin was and what happened. That was the purpose of the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Certainly. Just another question in relation to this: From the beginning of the interview and throughout, did you ever say to Mr. Borovcanin that there was a possibility that he could be under Article 7(3) of the Statute suspected of having committed these crimes, namely, that what he said throughout the interview about other persons could also be attributed to him?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Well, I've said to him then, "everything you say could be recorded and could be used in evidence against you in a later Tribunal proceeding including a trial."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Naturally, just to remind ourselves, that the words "against you" were not translated to Mr. Borovcanin at the outset, correct?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You didn't know that at the time, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only found that out when I was sitting here, Your Honour, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Graham I'm not holding it against you, not at all. I'm sure that it wasn't your error. However, it is clear that Mr. Borovcanin did not hear the caution as you uttered it in English, and I'm not saying that it was your fault or that you omitted it deliberately or anything of the sort. Today, in examination-in-chief, you said that Mr. Borovcanin said at the outset that he had engaged counsel, and you asked him twice whether he wanted to continue the interview without the presence of his counsel and that he consented to it, correct?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Yes. I asked him when we first met, but obviously there was no normal record of that which is why I repeated it in the interview, to make it very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When Mr. Borovcanin, and in the course of the interview, said to you in relation to his education and career what he said to you, could we agree that Mr. Borovcanin has no legal training whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't know that there is any foundation that other than what Mr. -- unless I'm missing something, I don't see there is any foundation for that question. Mr. Borovcanin told him he was a Professor at police academy but that doesn't follow that they had a discussion about his other training or his educational background.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see your point. Obviously the whole thing boils down to the following question: Apart from what we have in the transcript, were there other things said that were not recorded and consequently do not show up in the transcript? That's the fundamental thing that has to be answered. If not, I think we can proceed with your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, there is not any such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: But on this issue I believe that my colleague can stipulate that Mr. Borovcanin is not a lawyer by profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not stipulating to anything along those lines, Your Honour. The reference here just for the transcript is page 4, lines 15 to 18 and line 17, Mr. Borovcanin says, "At the moment I work as a Professor, as a lecturer at the police academy in Banja Luka." And it wouldn't surprise me whatsoever if some component of being a Professor at a police academy as having some legal background. Normally it would in systems I'm familiar with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic did ask Mr. Graham whether he has a law degree, so I think we are back to square 1. Let's proceed, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, just for the benefits of my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No questions were asked whether being a Professor at the police academy in Banja Luka entailed having a law degree or not, or whether there had been any legal training or not. If no question was asked, there was obviously no question answered. So where do you get from there? No where.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just my point was -- the initial question was, "Could we agree that Mr. Borovcanin had no legal training whatsoever," and then he went to the stipulation to mean that I don't accept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's why I asked whether there was anything else said apart from what we have in the transcript, because that I would accept then after that but, Mr. Lazarevic, take my advice, go ahead with your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I will -- as always, I'll take Your Honour's advice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Graham, on the basis of the fact that Mr. Borovcanin engaged counsel, could we consider that he believed he needed legal assistance during his interview with the OTP?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: I take it that he decided he didn't need it, that he was happy to start without it, because if he said he wanted it there, I certainly would not have commenced the interview.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have any idea at how come he attended the interview already assisted by counsel, who would have advised him about that right, if at all? Or was it something spontaneous? How did Mr. Bubic end up there? Was he recruited by the Tribunal's office for him? Was he selected by him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no background knowledge to it other than the fact that he was due to attend but was at court that morning and Mr. Borovcanin arrived without him and said he was happy to start before he arrived, but I don't know how he came to recruit the particular lawyer in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Borovcanin -- Mr. Lazarevic, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I will proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you proceed, one thing: Did you get a clue, an indication, as to whether Mr. Borovcanin had an opportunity to meet with Mr. Bubic before the first interview took place or before he met with you any way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I deliberately did not ask that question. I viewed it as legal privilege, and I didn't want to know what discussions he's had with his lawyer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But not even whether he had encountered, whether he had met with his lawyer, as you put it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't ask the question so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In the beginning of that first interview, Mr. Borovcanin asked to have a copy of the interview tape. You said that would you do it -- provide it as soon as possible. Do you remember that part of your evidence, Mr. Nicholls led you through it?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We can also agree that the interview started in the absence of the lawyer Mr. Borovcanin hired?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Based on the information I have, which is identical to the information in the possession of the OTP, the interview went until 20.37 and -- or 10.37 and then because the tape ran out you continued at 10.42, correct?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: I'm happy to accept that. I don't have that page in front of me, but I'm happy to accept that that's the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Can we have page 23 of this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not objecting. I just want to be -- I'm not sure what the question was exactly, if it's where the first break was or where the tape first ran out and had to be flipped over. It's slightly different but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The way I understood the question was what time the first session ended, what time, it was resumed, and presumably that's in relation to the presence or absence of Mr. Bubic, as I understand it. It's an hour and a half, 90 minute tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise because I've just read through the transcript, and in here it says 10.37 and it's actually 10.42 that I'm referring at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One question: Do you remember what kind of a tape was used, whether it was a 90 minute tape, a 60 minute tape or longer, and my next question is was the tape on all the time or would it be stopped when there was a pause; for example, say a pause of one minute or a few seconds or half a minute? Would you pause the tape or let it run?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I ever paused the tape I would comment on the tape. So if it's not commented on it would be allowed to run. I would never pause where nothing would be taped. And as for the length of the tape, 90 minutes was the norm, 120s were viewed as too long, so it would be either a 90 or a 60 minute tape as a rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just to be precise, drawing the Court attention to pages 11 and 12, the tape was flipped over at 9.45. So it was a 45 minute-sided tape, and we have the original tapes here. The interview began again at 9.46, immediately after the tape was flipped. And according to the transcript, the first break is at 10.27 resuming at 10.42.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it's a 90 minute tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not giving evidence but it looks like it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: At any rate, the issue of flipping the tape was not important to me at all. I simply referred to it so as to give a clear indication to my learned friends. At any page, on page 21 of the transcript, it says that the tape has run out and that a new tape would be inserted and then the interview begins at 10.42, which is page 23 of the transcript. At that point, you gave the following caution to Mr. Borovcanin which I will read in English. "You do not have to answer any of our questions [In English] unless you want to. Anything you say will be recorded and could be used in evidence in later Tribunal proceedings. And of course your right to legal representation continues and your lawyer still has not arrived at this location, so if at any time you want to stop the interview, please do so." [Interpretation] And Mr. Borovcanin agreed to continue without his lawyer being present, correct?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If we were to look at this caution again, the caution given to Mr. Borovcanin, the one that I have just read out, we can see that once again, you did not tell him explicitly that he didn't need to talk to you at all, that he was free to go at any moment, just leave the room, correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, I don't think the question, Mr. Lazarevic, I would split it in two. The first one is whether he told him that he was free not to answer any question, and secondly whether he told him that he could also leave the room. Because that was split before, and it should be split again now, especially considering the witness's answer to both questions before.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I'm reminding Mr. Borovcanin of his rights, I do tell him you do not have to answer any of your questions unless you want to. In terms of telling him he's free to leave the room, as I say, as an investigator I have no power of arrest that would be just arresting somebody. And he's just been out on a fresh air break as we say at the start, so it didn't seem like it was something I needed to say at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Mr. Graham, that's not what I had in mind. What I had in mind was the situation where Mr. Borovcanin would simply stand up and leave the room. He was entitled to do that, and you didn't inform him of that. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: I haven't said those words in the environment and the set up and the level of my powers, I didn't see -- deem it necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Very well. On this occasion, when you uttered the caution, you did not tell him that whatever Mr. Borovcanin said could be used in the proceedings against him. So this is not a case of imprecise interpretation. Rather, in the English transcript, we can see that you did not utter the words, "Against you"; is that right? Would you please look at it again?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: No, I've not uttered those words.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Did you use the same aide-memoire, the one you used the first time you cautioned Mr. Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: It will have been on the table, but I've not read it out verbatim. This is a 15 minute break of a continuing interview. Just to remind Mr. Borovcanin that his rights were the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But if I'm following you closely, you did not say to him that he had the same rights. You did not draw his attention to that fact.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: I've said because we've had a break, it's just to remind you of your rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: At any rate, the conversation between you and Mr. Borovcanin went on, and it was interrupted at 11.59 as you mentioned in examination-in-chief because Mr. Zoran Bubic, Mr. Borovcanin's lawyer, arrived, correct?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Yes. I think I had just started a new tape when the note came under the door, and I stopped that tape and started a fresh one again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's precisely what I suggested. When Mr. Bubic arrived and when you made a break, this break lasted for about two hours and then at 1406 the interview was continued. For your reference this can be found on page 46 -- 43 of the transcript. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Today, when being examined by Mr. Nicholls, you said that you did not know Mr. Zoran Bubic from before. He was the then-lawyer of Mr. Borovcanin. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Graham.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. This is the second time. I think it's Goran Bubic and counsel is saying"Zoran." I just draw his attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you're right. Yes. Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure that's not the question I was asked, I thought I was asked if I knew Mr. Borovcanin before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It could have been a translation error.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I clarify this Your Honour. It's a very simple one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: See here, Mr. Graham, during these interviews that you had with Mr. Borovcanin, he was represented by two different lawyers, correct?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: I don't recall. I -- if it's on the transcript then I'm more than happy to accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It stems from the transcript, and this is yet another thing that Mr. Nicholls could stipulate, is that there were two lawyers, Goran Bubic and Zoran Bubic. They have identical last names and very similar first names, so perhaps this is what is creating the confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is certainly not what's in a names case. Are you prepared to stipulate that, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to -- I just -- I don't know, Your Honour, at this point if it was two with the same name and they -- I've been going off the transcript where we have the same name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, if you had stated this before Mr. Meek as being the reason why you wanted to bring Mr. McCloskey as a witness, perhaps you would have stood a better chance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Never too late, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Graham, let's try to simplify it, during -- you were there during the both interviews all the time, weren't you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing one lawyer there or two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have a memory of one, but if I -- just to clarify it, on this date I conducted four interviews with three different people. So in the lunchtime break there was an interview, and I can't remember if that person had a lawyer. And at the end of the interviews on the 20th there was also a further interview so which lawyer was which, after five years, I have no recollection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the second interview, was it the same lawyer you had seen in the first interview that assisted Mr. Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only have a recollection of one lawyer being in the room.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, I must admit this is not the information that I had but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does it help your case if he had two lawyers instead of one?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I think I'll be able to clarify this, and we will probably find a solution in our discussion. But this is not of crucial importance at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So next -- your next question. We have got five minutes to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just to clarify another matter in relation to this: In the course of the interview, there was just one lawyer present, there were not two lawyers there at the same time, were there?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: I have no recollection of two lawyers being present in the room at the same time for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that we've managed to clarify at least something. And you have already said that you did not know the gentleman previously, the one that was present during the interview?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: I don't recollect knowing him. Whether he'd sat on a previous interview I had done, I certainly can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: The continuation of the interview on the 20th of February 2002, which begins on page 43, the one that we have just referred to, you once again gave caution to Mr. Borovcanin, which can be found on page 43 and 44. You can see it right now. Do you have it before you?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we observe that once again, Mr. Borovcanin did not receive the translation of the words "against you"?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And naturally, you will see that once again, the following words were used, "May become a possible suspect." At least that's how it was translated to Mr. Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: I think it says "you may be a suspect" on this, page 44.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm now quoting to you what was translated to Mr. Borovcanin in B/C/S, and that can be found in the B/C/S transcript. This is what was conveyed to Mr. Borovcanin and perhaps I'm expecting too much of you, hoping that you would know what was translated to Mr. Borovcanin. But I'm just trying to ascertain what he heard out of what you said. But let us go back once again to Mr. Borovcanin's counsel, Mr. Bubic. He arrived and the interview continued. Did Mr. Bubic ask you at the beginning of the interview, this cannot be seen in the transcript and that's why I'm asking you this, did he ask you whether his client, that is to say Mr. Borovcanin, consented to the interview in the absence of his lawyer?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: I don't recall having any conversation with the lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: All right. But can we agree that in the transcript, which is before us, and which is a record of the interview, it doesn't say that -- it doesn't show that Mr. Bubic asked you at any point whether his client consented to have the interview in absence of his lawyer, it's not reflected anywhere in the transcript, correct?

utterances.speaker: ALISTAIR GRAHAM.
utterances.text: No, it's not in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we need to stop here for the day. We'll resume tomorrow in the afternoon at 2.15. Thank you so much. One moment, yes. Mr. Graham, this is addressed to you. I'm telling you this not because I don't believe you are aware of the rule but since you are familiar with this Tribunal, and you probably have a lot of friends here still, I need to confirm that you need -- you cannot liaise with anyone or discuss the substance of your testimony with anyone between now and tomorrow when we proceed. I have your word for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
